title: The dental nurse at chairside & four-handed dentistry
blurb: Clock positions, instrument transfer, patient positioning and keeping the patient safe while the dentist works.
question: You are assisting a right-handed dentist with a Class II filling. The dentist holds out a hand for the next instrument while the patient suddenly closes on the matrix band. Where should you be sitting, how do you pass instruments, and what do you do first about the patient biting down?

teach.body: Four-handed dentistry means the dentist and dental nurse work as one team at the chair. The dentist keeps their eyes on the mouth and their hands in the working area. You anticipate what comes next, pass and receive instruments, keep the field clear with suction and retraction, mix materials at the right moment and watch the patient. Done well, treatment is quicker, safer and less tiring for everyone, and the patient feels looked after.

head: Zone
Right-handed
Left-handed
Used for
teach.caption: Picture a clock laid over the chair from above, with 12 o'clock behind the patient's head. For a left-handed dentist everything is mirrored. Textbooks vary slightly on the exact ranges; this lesson uses one common convention throughout.

teach.h: Why the transfer zone is over the chest
teach.body: Instruments are passed below the patient's chin, over the chest, never over the face. If something is dropped it lands on the bib, not in the eyes. Sit close to the patient with your knees towards their head, hips level with their shoulders, and your eye level slightly higher than the dentist's so you can see into the mouth. Your left hand passes instruments; your right hand holds the aspirator (for a right-handed dentist).

teach.h: Passing an instrument: the parallel exchange

steps.label: Anticipate
steps.sub: Have the next instrument ready in your left hand

steps.label: Hold it correctly
steps.sub: Grip the non-working end, working end pointing to the arch

steps.label: Meet in the transfer zone
steps.sub: Bring it parallel to the used instrument

steps.label: Take the used one
steps.sub: Hook it with your little finger

steps.label: Deliver
steps.sub: Place the new handle firmly into the dentist's fingers

steps.label: Return to tray
steps.sub: Put the used one back in order of use

teach.caption: The dentist should not need to look away from the mouth. A mouth mirror and probe are passed first at the start of almost every procedure.

teach.note: Sharps are placed on a tray (a neutral zone) for the dentist to pick up, not passed hand to hand, to cut the risk of a sharps injury.

rows.label: Position
values: Lying back, head about level with knees
Back raised, sitting partly or fully up

rows.label: Also for
values: A patient who feels faint (legs raised)

teach.caption: Supine tips: for the upper arch tilt the head back; for the lower arch bring the chin down. Raise the patient slowly at the end of treatment: sitting up too fast can make them dizzy (postural hypotension). In late pregnancy, avoid lying flat; tilt the patient slightly to the left.

teach.body: Before treatment: give the patient safety glasses and a bib, and check they are comfortable. Switch the light on aimed at the chest, then move it up to the mouth so it never shines in the eyes. During treatment: aspirate, retract the cheek or tongue, keep the mirror clear with air, mix materials when asked and keep the dentist's view open. Throughout: watch the patient's colour, breathing and body language, and agree a stop signal, such as a raised hand.

teach.h: The patient closes with instruments in the mouth

steps.label: Withdraw safely
steps.sub: Remove instruments without dragging over soft tissue

steps.label: Check for injury
steps.sub: Lips, tongue, cheeks, and the instrument itself

steps.label: Reassure and rest
steps.sub: Offer a short break before carrying on

teach.caption: If the patient keeps closing, they are usually tired or anxious. Short rests help; the dentist may also suggest a mouth prop.

teach.text: Don't pull an instrument out sharply or keep working when a patient bites down. Withdraw safely and check for injury FIRST. And never pass anything over the patient's face: the transfer zone is over the chest.

items: Right-handed dentist: operator 7 to 12, static 12 to 2, nurse 2 to 4, transfer 4 to 7 o'clock.
Pass with your left hand in the transfer zone using a parallel exchange; take the used instrument with your little finger.
Mirror and probe come first. Sharps go via a neutral zone, not hand to hand.
Supine for most treatment; more upright for impressions, breathlessness and late pregnancy.
Patient closes on instruments: stop, withdraw safely, check for injury, reassure, offer rests.

summary: You can now position yourself, the dentist and the patient correctly for four-handed dentistry, pass and receive instruments safely in the transfer zone, decide what goes via a neutral zone, and respond calmly and safely when a patient closes on instruments.

A.q: You are assisting a right-handed dentist. In which clock zone should you normally sit?
options: 7 to 12 o'clock
12 to 2 o'clock
2 to 4 o'clock
4 to 7 o'clock
A.why: For a right-handed operator the dental nurse sits in the assistant's zone, 2 to 4 o'clock, with the patient's head at 12.

whyNot.0: 7 to 12 o'clock is the operator's zone, where the dentist sits.
whyNot.1: 12 to 2 o'clock is the static zone, used for the mobile cabinet and items not passed.
whyNot.3: 4 to 7 o'clock is the transfer zone, where instruments pass over the patient's chest.

A.q: A patient bites down suddenly while the dentist is fitting a matrix band. What should you do first?
options: Ask the patient to open wider and carry on
Withdraw instruments safely; check for injury
Place a mouth prop straight away without asking
Record the incident in the accident book
A.why: Patient safety comes first: stop, withdraw instruments carefully and check the soft tissues for injury before going on.

whyNot.0: Carrying on risks injury to the patient; something may already be damaged.
whyNot.2: A prop may help later, but it needs explaining and agreeing, and the immediate priority is safe withdrawal.
whyNot.3: Recording comes later, and only if there was an injury or incident.

A.q: Why are instruments passed over the patient's chest rather than their face?
options: It keeps the operating light unobstructed
Anything dropped won't land on the face or eyes
It lets the patient see each instrument coming
It keeps instruments within reach of the suction
A.why: The transfer zone sits below the chin so that anything dropped falls onto the bib rather than into the patient's eyes or face.

whyNot.0: The light is positioned separately; the reason for the transfer zone is patient safety.
whyNot.2: Seeing instruments approach can make patients more anxious, and it isn't the purpose.
whyNot.3: The suction is in the nurse's other hand and works in the mouth, not the transfer zone.

B.q: The dentist starts a routine filling and holds out a hand for the first instrument. Which is usually passed first?
options: Mouth mirror
Excavator
Flat plastic
Burnisher
B.why: A mouth mirror (with a probe) is passed first: the dentist needs to see, retract and examine before anything else.

whyNot.1: An excavator removes soft caries, later in the procedure.
whyNot.2: A flat plastic places material near the end of the procedure.
whyNot.3: A burnisher smooths amalgam after packing, near the end.

B.q: During a parallel instrument exchange, how does the nurse usually take back the used instrument?
options: By grasping its working end
By asking the dentist to put it down
By hooking it with the little finger
By taking it with the suction hand
B.why: The little finger of the passing hand hooks the used instrument while the thumb and fingers deliver the new one, so the exchange takes one smooth movement.

whyNot.0: Grasping a contaminated working end risks injury and is unhygienic.
whyNot.1: The point of four-handed dentistry is that the dentist does not have to look away or put things down.
whyNot.3: The other hand stays on the aspirator to keep the field clear.

B.q: A patient in the later stages of pregnancy feels dizzy lying flat. What position change is most appropriate?
options: Lower the head further, below the level of the knees
Sit them partly up, tilted to the left
Raise both legs high above the chest
Turn them face down until they recover
B.why: Lying flat late in pregnancy can press on major blood vessels; sitting partly up with a slight left tilt relieves this.

whyNot.0: Lowering the head further increases pressure on the vessels in late pregnancy.
whyNot.2: Raising the legs is used for a simple faint, not for pressure from the pregnant uterus.
whyNot.3: A face-down position is unsafe and impractical in a dental chair.

C.q: Which zone holds the mobile cabinet and items that are not passed during treatment, for a right-handed dentist?
options: The transfer zone, 4 to 7
The operator's zone, 7 to 12
The assistant's zone, 2 to 4
The static zone, 12 to 2
C.why: The static zone, 12 to 2 o'clock behind the patient's head, holds equipment and items not handed over during the procedure.

whyNot.0: The transfer zone is where instruments are passed, over the chest.
whyNot.1: The operator's zone is where the dentist sits.
whyNot.2: The assistant's zone is where the nurse sits.

C.q: A patient keeps closing their mouth during a long restoration. What is the best supportive action?
options: Offer short rests during the procedure
Tell the patient to concentrate harder
Work faster to finish before they tire
Hold the patient's jaw open firmly
C.why: Repeated closing usually means the patient is tired or anxious. Short, planned rests help them cope and keep them safe.

whyNot.1: Blaming the patient increases anxiety and doesn't address tiredness.
whyNot.2: Rushing increases the risk of mistakes and injury.
whyNot.3: Forcing the jaw is unsafe and unacceptable without consent.

C.q: How should a loaded local anaesthetic syringe be handed to the dentist?
options: Hand to hand, needle pointing at the dentist
Over the patient's face for speed
Placed in a neutral zone for them to pick up
Passed by the patient to the dentist
C.why: Sharps such as LA syringes and scalpels are placed in a neutral zone rather than passed hand to hand, cutting the risk of a sharps injury.

whyNot.0: Passing a needle hand to hand, especially pointing at someone, is a sharps injury risk.
whyNot.1: Nothing is ever passed over the patient's face.
whyNot.3: The patient should never handle instruments.

reteach.title: Think of a relay race
reteach.question: A relay team wins by smooth baton changes in a fixed zone. How is passing instruments at the chair like a relay handover?

blocks.h: Same zone, same hand, every time
blocks.body: In a relay, the baton always changes hands in the same zone, and the runner receiving it doesn't look back. At the chair, the transfer zone over the chest is your changeover zone. The dentist keeps looking at the tooth; you put the instrument into their hand the right way round and take the used one with your little finger. Sharp batons, like needles and scalpels, are never thrown: they are put down in a neutral zone.

blocks.caption: The dentist sits on the patient's right, the nurse on the patient's left, and instruments meet over the chest.

blocks.text: If the patient bites down, the race stops. Withdraw safely, check for injury, then reassure and rest.

explain.body: With the patient's head at 12 o'clock, a right-handed dentist sits from 7 to 12, the nurse from 2 to 4, instruments pass in the transfer zone from 4 to 7, and the static zone from 12 to 2 holds items not passed. For a left-handed dentist it is all mirrored.

test.q: For a LEFT-handed dentist, where does the dental nurse usually sit?
options: 2 to 4 o'clock
8 to 10 o'clock
12 to 2 o'clock
4 to 7 o'clock
test.why: For a left-handed operator everything is mirrored, so the nurse moves to the 8 to 10 o'clock zone.

whyNot.0: 2 to 4 is the nurse's zone for a right-handed dentist.
whyNot.2: 12 to 2 is the static zone for a right-handed dentist.
whyNot.3: 4 to 7 is the right-handed transfer zone.

explain.body: Hold the next instrument by its non-working end in your left hand, working end pointing towards the arch being treated. Meet the dentist's hand in the transfer zone, parallel to the used instrument, hook the used one with your little finger and press the new handle into their fingers. Mirror and probe go first; sharps go via a neutral zone.

rows.label: Hand a scalpel hand to hand

test.q: The dentist is working on an upper molar. How should you orient the instrument as you pass it?
options: Working end pointing down
Working end pointing towards you
Working end pointing up
Handle first, working end hidden
test.why: The working end is pointed towards the arch being treated, so for upper teeth it points upwards and the dentist can use it straight away.

whyNot.0: Pointing down suits the lower arch.
whyNot.1: Pointing it at yourself means the dentist has to turn it round.
whyNot.3: The handle goes into the dentist's fingers, but the working end must already face the right arch.

explain.body: Most treatment is done supine. For the upper arch the head tilts back; for the lower arch the chin comes down. Sit patients more upright for impressions, breathlessness and late pregnancy (with a slight left tilt). Bring them up slowly at the end to avoid dizziness.

test.q: Why should you raise a patient slowly at the end of a long appointment?
options: To stop the chair motor overheating on the way up
To prevent dizziness from postural hypotension
To give materials longer to set
To let the dentist write up notes first
test.why: Sitting up quickly after lying back can drop blood pressure briefly (postural hypotension), making the patient dizzy or faint.

whyNot.0: The chair motor isn't the reason; patient safety is.
whyNot.2: Setting times don't depend on chair position.
whyNot.3: Notes can be written at any time; the slow rise is for the patient.

explain.body: Agree a stop signal before you start. Watch the patient's colour, breathing and expression. If they close on instruments, stop, withdraw safely and check for injury before carrying on. If they keep closing, offer short rests.

test.q: The patient closes onto a probe mid-examination. Which response is best?
options: Pull the probe out quickly
Ask them to bite harder so the probe stays still
Carry on and check at the end
Withdraw it carefully and check for injury
test.why: Careful withdrawal and an injury check protect the patient; then reassure and continue when ready.

whyNot.0: Yanking an instrument out can cut the lips, tongue or cheek.
whyNot.1: Biting harder makes injury more likely.
whyNot.2: Any injury needs dealing with straight away, not at the end.
